newsitem.title: UK: UK's Portillo backs government line over Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Portillo backs government line over Europe.

text.p: British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said on Thursday he backed the government's policy of leaving the option open of joining a single European currency.

Asked if he could ever envisage voting for British membership of European economic and monetary union, Portillo told BBC radio: "I am unshakeable in my support for the Prime Minister and the government's policy. We are all members of the cabinet and we have made a common decision."
Portillo cryptically said that was the only reply he would ever give to that question.
Leading Conservative politician John Redwood told the same programme that the vast majority of his party were against a single European currency.
"The overwhelming majority of the Conservative Party...is instinctively against the abolition of the pound," Redwood said.
"This is a huge issue. It goes to the heart of what a country is and how a democracy operates," he said.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister John Major lit up the election campaign with an impassioned defence of his policy over Europe. He said two of his junior ministers had been reprimanded for abandoning the government's line in personal manifestos.
Later, in a hastily recorded television message, Major asked voters not to "tie his hands" in negotiations with European Union leaders by calling for EMU to be rejected now.
Redwood, a former minister and noted Eurosceptic, said a single currency would inevitably mean loss of sovereignty.
Latest opinion polls put the ruling Conservatives 17 points behind opposition Labour with election day only two days away -- a seemingly unbridgeable gap.

Portillo said a Labour government led by Tony Blair would surrender British sovereignty at the June meeting of EU leaders in Amsterdam. "We are sleepwalking towards an election with one party proposing to give up national sovereignty in June."
He said Blair would give up Britain's veto over "vital" interests.

A MORI poll in The Times newspaper showed 58 percent of voters would oppose Britain joining EMU if a referendum was held today. Both the Conservatives and Labour have promised a referendum before joining EMU.
